newsitem.title: UK: Softs Outlook - Cocoa, sugar seen prone to falls.
newsitem.headline: Softs Outlook - Cocoa, sugar seen prone to falls.

text.p: Devoid of keen funds and industry interest, LIFFE soft futures contracts are poised for further downside moves this week with sugar and cocoa leading the way. Cocoa, having breached initial chart downside goals, might face more losses amid thin pre-holiday trade while white sugar remained bearish under the weight of supply, traders said.
But coffee could provide some contrast as London took the lead from volatile New York arabica futures.

Prospects for the white sugar market were still bearish given supplies. Although some fund players would have to cover short March positions, sell stops placed around $301.00 a tonne should cap most of the short-term gains.
"If it starts taking a hit above $300, people will be looking to sell," said one trader.
"But they're not going to be inclined to be too aggressive with the selling...especially if it is fund short covering -- they'll want to sell it on a scale-up basis," he said.

Supply of quality white sugar was not a problem, especially as the European Union, whose supply of C-quota sugar reached its traditional peak in December, was pushing out a lot of sugar through its weekly tenders. The spot white/raw premium should again be closely monitored this week and was likely to continue to narrow as a result of a pressured whites market coupled with the raws edging higher.
Some traders had forecast $60 by the end of the year.
But business was still likely to be quiet despite the trickle of pre-Ramadan physical demand from Middle East and North African buyers.
"There are parcels of business being done and while that's there it keeps the market ticking over," the trader said.
"You may have odd upticks on the market but overall it's rather bearish."
In coffee, traders expected some fireworks on Wednesday, when New York's spot December coffee contract expires.

Traders were also are awaiting a stream of stock data from New York and London on Monday, which could provide fresh impetus. The U.S. Green Coffee Association is due to release the November inventory figures on Monday, along with LIFFE's November certified coffee stock data. The data follow Friday's key U.S. Department of Agriculture's coffee crop balance.
Traders said the USDA report for coffee output in the current 1996/97 season contained no real surprises but projections for Mexico and some Central American countries came in strongly.
New York's Dec/March spread remained at a healthy level while the open interest on December was still relatively high against the almost non-existent certified stocks.
London coffee futures could rise but were not likely to gain as much as New York, although the differentials between the two markets had widened to around 51 cents last week from 47-47.50.
Fresh funds interest would emerge if January hit above $1,350 a tonne while roasters were well covered on the nearbys and were holding back purchases until after Christmas.
LIFFE cocoa broke through key 920 stg a tonne support on Friday to trade as low as 917, but remained in its range between 900 and 950.

But given the slim volume, cocoa was seen likely to drift lower. "It is is coming off. Unfortunately the activity on cocoa has been so little. I think the only room on the market is down," said one trader.

Last week's comments by Robert Fish of PCR Ltd, who saw the Ivorian crop at a minimum of one million tonnes, turned sentiment slightly after an earlier projection by an Ivorian diplomat of between 850,000 and 900,000 tonnes.
Besides sterling's movements against major units, cocoa's immediate direction also hinged on West African crop arrivals as traders tried to gauge the size of the current harvest.
Broker GNI said the market would soar if the Ivorian and Ghanaian arrivals continued slow for a few more weeks.
